cases.title: Inlay Pathar: Adivasi farmland taken for a Hyatt hotel at Kaziranga
cases.place: Inlay Pathar, near Kohora, Golaghat district, Assam, India
cases.point: Kohora, the village on the edge of Kaziranga National Park in Bokakhat subdivision, Golaghat district; the Inlay Pathar fields in dispute lie on its fringe.

lenders.name: Hyatt Hotels Corporation (foreign investor, through its affiliate Two Seas Holdings)
lenders.role: When Juniper Hotels Limited, the Indian company that runs hotels under the Hyatt brand, filed for its Indian listing, Two Seas Holdings Ltd, described as an affiliate of Hyatt Hotels Corporation, held 50% of it (Zee Business). Down To Earth reports that Hyatt signed a memorandum of understanding with the Assam government on 23 September 2023 and that the hotel is to be owned by Hyatt; the state's press communique gave an investment of Rs 100 crore for 120-odd rooms on about 30 acres.

cases.conditions: The state supplies the land. The Bokakhat circle officer summoned the farmer Lokhu Gowala to a hearing on 31 May 2024; the notice stated that the land belonged to the Assam Tourism Development Corporation. The circle officer, Champak Deka, told Down To Earth that the land was turned into patta land after being handed to the corporation in 2022 and that the construction on it was illegal because it was government land. Farmers say revenue collection on their plots stopped in 2022 and that the district administration installed pillars on their land towards the end of 2023 (Down To Earth). No loan or lender condition was found.

companies.name: Hyatt Hotels Corporation
companies.role: Named by Down To Earth as the owner of the planned hotel, part-owner of the developer through its affiliate Two Seas Holdings, and signatory of the September 2023 memorandum with the Assam government
companies.desc: United States hotel group. When Juniper Hotels filed for its Indian listing, Hyatt's affiliate Two Seas Holdings held 50% of the company, which ran seven hotels and serviced apartments with 1,836 keys under the Hyatt brand (Zee Business).

companies.name: Juniper Hotels Limited
companies.role: Developer of the hotel in partnership with the Assam Tourism Development Corporation, according to the complaint
companies.desc: Indian hotel company owned 50% by Hyatt's affiliate Two Seas Holdings, 44.68% by Saraf Hotels and 5.32% by Juniper Investments (Zee Business).

cases.community: Down To Earth reported in 2024 that the Assam government deems about 60 farmers on the site illegal encroachers, while the activist Pranab Doley counts 45-odd families who have farmed there for generations; the farmers say they have collectively farmed over 30 acres. Lokhu Gowala farms six bighas, 1.9 acres, of paddy and says he paid annual patta revenue for more than a decade; Minali Gowala has about seven bighas, 2.3 acres; Jogeshwar Gowala is likely to lose about three bighas, one acre. On 7 June 2024 the Golaghat district administration tore down Lokhu Gowala's house. He had been summoned to a hearing on the land and was told the circle officer was not available. The Quint put the site at 60 bighas, about 37 acres, of farmland worked by about 45 Adivasi families.
cases.suppression: Assam police arrested Pranab Doley and at least four other people on 12 July 2026, the day before about 30 people began an indefinite strike demanding their release on 13 July; the community says the police charges are unfounded (The Quint). The Wire reported on 30 July 2026 that Doley was in judicial custody. The Quint does not say what the charges were.
cases.outcome: The complaint was filed with the United States contact point on 30 March 2026; OECD Watch records no assessment, and the full complaint text has not been disclosed under the contact point's confidentiality requirements. A committee appointed by India's Supreme Court found on a visit in 2018 that more than 22 structures stood on the animal corridors connecting Kaziranga with the Karbi Anglong landscape, and in April 2019 the Supreme Court banned construction of any kind on private land forming part of those corridors (Down To Earth). Down To Earth reported in June 2024 that Hyatt had not officially announced the construction. The Wire described the hotel as a proposed project on 30 July 2026 and reported the families saying they will keep resisting the acquisition of their land.

cases.confidence_note: Two national Indian outlets record the harm outside the complaint: Down To Earth the demolition of 7 June 2024 and the families' holdings, The Quint and The Wire the July 2026 arrests. The complaint text itself is confidential. Down To Earth names Hyatt's September 2023 memorandum with the state, says the hotel is to be owned by Hyatt and says Hyatt has not officially announced the project; it does not mention Juniper Hotels, while the complaint names Juniper as developer and Hyatt as brander, operator and investor. Down To Earth carries no comment from Hyatt or Juniper. The Zee Business report of Juniper's listing papers carries no date on the page, so none is given here. The Quint spells the site Inglay Pathar and Down To Earth spells it Inlay Pathar. A separate Taj resort is planned on eight hectares of the nearby Hathikhuli tea estate, so the two projects should not be confused. The Wire's page is built by script and only its headline and standfirst were served, to the checker and on a second attempt from the main session, so the two facts taken from it, the judicial custody and that families are still resisting, rest on that standfirst and not on the article body. The Quint carries the arrests independently.
cases.ecosystem: The site lies on the fringe of Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage site, about 2 km from the park by The Quint's account, and the complainants place it in an animal corridor and less than 1 km from the park. The land borders the Golaghat and Karbi Anglong districts and is used by elephants, tigers, leopards, deer and rhino moving to higher ground during floods (Down To Earth). The Supreme Court's committee counted more than 22 structures on the Kaziranga-Karbi Anglong corridors in 2018, and the court banned further construction on private corridor land in April 2019.
cx: Anonymous civil society organisation vs. Hyatt Hotels Corporation

cases.whole: Nothing has opened. The figures for the project are the state's own: Rs 100 crore, 120-odd rooms, swimming pools and large parking spaces on about 30 acres, from the Assam government publicity department's communique reported by Down To Earth. The Quint reported on 25 July 2026 that activists say the project will hit the livelihoods of the families who farm the land and leave hundreds of other local people jobless.

cases.title: Yavatmal cotton sprayers and Syngenta's Polo
cases.point: Yavatmal town in Vidarbha, where the government hospital took in most of the serious poisoning cases from the surrounding cotton villages.

lenders.name: Syngenta AG (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Swiss maker of the insecticide Polo and owner of Syngenta India Ltd, through which it introduced Polo to the Indian market in 2008 (Down To Earth). Public Eye's investigation records exports of more than 126 tonnes of diafenthiuron from Switzerland in 2017, of which 75 tonnes went to India, 50 to South Africa and 1.5 to Colombia.

cases.conditions: A product sale, not a loan. Diafenthiuron, Polo's active ingredient, was banned in the European Union in 2002 and in Switzerland in 2009 and was still being exported to India in 2017 (Public Eye). Public Eye dates Maharashtra's provisional ban on the sale of five pesticides including diafenthiuron to June 2018; Down To Earth dates the state ban to 2017 and says it lasted two months, state governments being able to prohibit use only temporarily. The national list of twelve pesticides to be banned, published in August 2018, left diafenthiuron out (Public Eye). No lender condition was found.

companies.name: Syngenta AG
companies.desc: Swiss agrochemical and seed company. Public Eye's 2018 investigation records it exporting over 126 tonnes of diafenthiuron in 2017, a substance banned for use in Switzerland since 2009.

companies.name: Syngenta India Ltd
companies.role: Syngenta's Indian arm, through which Syngenta introduced Polo to the Indian market in 2008 (Down To Earth)
companies.desc: Named in the complaint alongside the Swiss parent. Its head of communications told Down To Earth in 2023 that neither Syngenta nor any Syngenta product was deemed responsible for the events in Yavatmal.

cases.community: Twenty-one farmers died of pesticide poisoning in Yavatmal district in 2017-18, the highest number recorded in any district in Maharashtra in that period, and 63 died across fifteen districts; the Special Investigation Team's report counted 886 patients hospitalised in Yavatmal (Down To Earth). Public Eye counted 800 farmers and agricultural workers admitted to hospital in Yavatmal with acute poisoning after spraying, several hundred of them temporarily blinded, and more than 50 men fatally poisoned across Vidarbha between July and October 2017. Police records list 96 of the poisoned as having used Polo, 60 with other pesticides and 36 with Polo alone (Down To Earth). The hospital in Yavatmal lacked knowledge of the substances in the pesticides and the diagnostic tools to identify them; serious cases were given atropine (Public Eye). The complainants add that household incomes fell, that women took on care of sick husbands alongside field labour at lower wages than men, and that 28 of the 51 farmers in the complaint report lasting neurological and muscular problems.
cases.killed_note: Not counted here. Twenty-one farmers died of pesticide poisoning in Yavatmal district in 2017-18 (Down To Earth). Public Eye records Bandu Chandrabhan Sonule, declared dead at 1.35 p.m. on 23 September 2017 at the government hospital in Yavatmal after spraying Polo mixed with other products, with an autopsy finding post-mortem findings consistent with death due to poisoning; Down To Earth records Shankar Nago Agalave, who sprayed Polo on 24 September 2017 and died five days later in a private hospital in Nagpur. Public Eye says it is impossible to say which substance or combination of substances was responsible, the state investigation team's report names monocrotophos and not Polo, Syngenta denies that Polo caused the poisonings, and the Basel civil court has not ruled, so no death is attributed to the company.
cases.outcome: The Maharashtra chief minister tasked a seven-person team of special investigators with finding the causes at the beginning of October 2017. It found cotton plants grown up to 1.8 metres tall, insect attacks worse than the previous year, spraying at head height which increased the proportion of pesticide entering the body through inhalation, mixing of insecticides with plant growth regulators, sprayers working without proper protective equipment, and information leaflet writing it found not legible; it recommended the agriculture department make protective equipment available to farmers and farm labourers through the state farm service centres, which Down To Earth reported in 2023 farmers still lacked. In October 2017 the state agriculture minister announced that investigations into Syngenta over Polo had been launched, with allegations of culpable homicide; Public Eye says it is not known whether that investigation ever took place. The Swiss contact point accepted the complaint on 15 December 2020 and its final statement of 16 June 2022 closed the question of whether Polo poisoned the 51 farmers, on the ground that discussing it would create serious prejudice for Syngenta in the Basel proceedings; it recommended Syngenta review its customer complaint process in India, and its follow-up of 15 June 2023 said Syngenta had made that process more accessible and transparent while the complainants said the mediation brought no compensation and no change to Syngenta's manufacturing and distribution (OECD Watch). Three families, the widows of two farmers and a farmer who survived severe poisoning, sued Syngenta in the Basel civil court in June 2021 under Swiss product liability law; the court granted them legal aid in June 2022 and, as reported on 30 June 2025, decided to begin assessing the evidence on the victims' use of Polo (Public Eye).

cases.confidence_note: The poisonings are recorded outside the complaint: the state Special Investigation Team counted 886 patients hospitalised in Yavatmal and Down To Earth, a national Indian magazine, reports 21 deaths in the district in 2017-18 and police records naming 96 poisoned people who had used Polo, 36 of them Polo alone. The link to Polo is disputed. The investigation team's report names monocrotophos and does not mention Polo. Public Eye says it is impossible to say which substance or combination was responsible in the cases it documents. Syngenta denies the health claims, said in October 2017 that there 'may have been other reasons' and pointed to plant height and farmer practice (Public Eye), said after the mediation that it regretted there was 'no meaningful dialogue' (SWI swissinfo.ch), and told Down To Earth in 2023 that it does not manufacture Polo. The Basel civil court has reached only the evidence stage. Two dates differ between sources: Public Eye puts the grant of legal aid in June 2022, Down To Earth at a hearing in August 2022; and Down To Earth dates Polo's introduction in India to 2008, while Syngenta's own October 2017 statement puts its use there at fourteen years.
cx: Public Eye et al. vs. Syngenta
Syngenta pesticide poisons Indian agricultural  workers
cases.whole: Syngenta said in October 2017 that Polo had been used by farmers across India for fourteen years with no reported incidents of fatal casualties; that is the company's own account and Public Eye records it alongside 75 tonnes of diafenthiuron shipped to India in 2017. Of the 51 farmers in the complaint, 43 were hospitalised, 44 reported temporary blindness and 16 were unconscious for between several hours and several days; most could not work for long periods and a few for up to a year. Those are the complainants' figures. The mediation ran from the contact point's acceptance in December 2020 to its final statement in June 2022 and produced a revised company complaints process in India and no compensation. Down To Earth reported in 2023 that Syngenta still exports and distributes in India a pesticide banned in Switzerland since 2009.

cases.title: Clearing inside the Ayoreo Totobiegosode reserve and the leather trade
cases.place: Ayoreo Totobiegosode Natural and Cultural Patrimony, Alto Paraguay, Paraguay
cases.point: Inside the Ayoreo Totobiegosode reserve (PNCAT), Puerto Casado district, Alto Paraguay, where the ranching firms cleared forest for cattle pasture.

lenders.name: Yaguarete Pora S.A. (foreign investor, Brazilian-owned)
lenders.role: Earthsight describes it as a Brazilian-owned cattle firm which acquired a title to 78,000 hectares inside PNCAT in 2002 and immediately pushed 60 kilometres of new roads into the forest; it cleared more than 2,000 hectares under a licence the environment ministry revoked in November 2008, and Earthsight records it clearing again after the licence was reissued in late 2013.

lenders.name: Caucasian SA (foreign investor, Brazilian)
lenders.role: Earthsight identifies this Brazilian firm as the one that carried out the largest area of recent clearance inside the reserve: 2,100 hectares north of Yaguarete Pora's land in 2018, and a further 663 hectares in October and November 2019 after an out-of-court settlement in late 2018 in which it had agreed to stop clearing and pay compensation.

cases.conditions: A purchase, not a loan. Mongabay reported in October 2021, quoting Earthsight, that the only investigation Pasubio admitted to was obtaining a blanket assurance from a Paraguayan ministry that Earthsight says does not have jurisdiction over the relevant laws. Pasubio's statement of 20 December 2023 makes future purchases conditional on a Paraguayan supplier giving guarantees that it has no relationship, direct or indirect, with the cattle ranches inside the reserve (Earthsight). The EU Deforestation Regulation was due to require firms to guarantee their leather was not linked to deforestation or illegalities in the country of production from the end of 2024.

companies.name: Gruppo Pasubio (Conceria Pasubio)
companies.role: Italian tannery buying Paraguayan hides and the company the complaint was filed against; agreed in December 2023 to halt commercial relations with Paraguayan suppliers that cannot give guarantees about ranches inside the reserve
companies.desc: Italian leather tannery. Earthsight calls it the leading importer of Paraguayan leather and the largest European buyer over the ten years to 2023, puts an estimated 39 per cent of Paraguay's leather exports as destined for it, and records it supplying vehicle interiors for cars made by BMW, Jaguar Land Rover, Volkswagen, Peugeot, Porsche and Citroen.

companies.name: Yaguarete Pora
companies.role: Took title to 78,000 hectares inside the reserve in 2002 and cleared forest there under licences granted in 2007 and late 2013
companies.desc: Cattle ranching company Earthsight describes as Brazilian-owned, fined $16,000 by a Paraguayan administrative court in 2010 for concealing information on the presence of uncontacted groups in its environmental impact assessment.

companies.name: Caucasian SA
companies.role: Cleared 2,100 hectares inside the reserve in 2018 and a further 663 hectares in October and November 2019
companies.desc: Brazilian cattle ranching firm whose land inside the reserve lies north of Yaguarete Pora's; Mongabay reports Earthsight recording more than 200 fires on it in 2020. Earthsight traced its cattle to the Minerva-owned FrigoAthena slaughterhouse.

companies.name: Cooperativa Chortitzer
companies.role: Acquired a ranch on the opposite side of the reserve in April 2019, shortly before about 520 hectares were cleared there that summer
companies.desc: Paraguayan Mennonite agricultural cooperative and meatpacker. Earthsight records all hides from Chortitzer being sold to Cencoprod, a tannery set up by Chortitzer and two other Mennonite slaughterhouses, and names Cencoprod as one of the three exporters whose leather it traced to Pasubio.

cases.community: The reserve is the land of the Ayoreo Totobiegosode, whom Earthsight describes as the only indigenous peoples living in voluntary isolation anywhere in the Americas outside the Amazon rainforest. By the end of 2019 some 530 square kilometres inside it had been cleared and stocked with cattle to produce beef and leather for export (Earthsight). The complainants say the loss of the forest they depend on for all their vital needs forces them to leave their land in search of food and care and into contact they have not chosen. Mongabay reported in October 2021, citing a lawyer for the Totobiegosode, that a group of uncontacted people approached a settled community in the south of the reserve at night in January and February 2021 and voiced concern about outsiders encroaching on their land.
cases.outcome: Paraguay's Comptroller General's Office audited Yaguarete Pora's clearing licence, concluded it had been issued illegally and lodged a criminal complaint with the state attorney general; the environment ministry revoked the licence in November 2008, by which time more than 2,000 hectares had gone; an administrative court fined the company $16,000 in 2010 for concealing information on the presence of uncontacted groups; the licence was reissued in late 2013 without new documentation; the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, through precautionary measure 54-13 in February 2016, ordered Paraguay to ensure the immediate cessation of deforestation on Totobiegosode land; and the forestry institute INFONA issued resolutions in February 2018 suspending all land use change plans granted to properties inside the reserve (Earthsight). Clearing continued after each step. The Italian contact point accepted Survival International's complaint on 6 December 2023; on 20 December 2023 both parties withdrew, saying they had reached an independent agreement, and Pasubio announced it would halt all commercial relationships with any Paraguayan supplier unable to give guarantees about ranches inside the reserve; the complaint was concluded on 15 February 2024 (OECD Watch). Earthsight says the pledge covers only this reserve, not other Paraguayan or Brazilian sources, and that Pasubio did not indicate how it will monitor whether its suppliers comply.

Report: luxury carmakers still sourcing deforestation-linked leather from Paraguay

cases.confidence_note: The clearing inside the reserve and the steps taken against it are on the record of Paraguayan state bodies and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, reported by Earthsight with satellite data and by Mongabay. The foreign link is the ownership of the ranches that cleared the land: Earthsight calls Yaguarete Pora Brazilian-owned and Caucasian SA a Brazilian firm. Pasubio, the company the complaint names, is a buyer of the hides rather than an owner or operator in Paraguay, and the trade link is Earthsight's own tracing of hides from the named ranches through three Paraguayan exporters to Pasubio. Earthsight records that no contact details could be found for Caucasian SA and that Yaguarete Pora and Chortitzer gave no response before publication; BMW said it had no information that its Latin American leather supply chains were affected, and Mongabay reports Jaguar Land Rover saying Pasubio had assured it that after extensive investigation it had not breached any national laws. Pasubio's December 2023 statement commits it to exclude such suppliers without accepting that it bought from them. Earthsight's own figures differ between reports: over 2,700 hectares for Caucasian SA across 2018-19 in the later summary against 2,100 plus 663 hectares in the detailed account, and over 500 against about 520 hectares at the Chortitzer ranch; its 2015 figure of a further 2,000 hectares for Yaguarete Pora may overlap the 5,500 hectares it gives for 2014 and 2015 together.
cases.ecosystem: The dry forest of the Paraguayan Chaco inside the reserve, the 550,000-hectare territory Paraguay formally recognised in 2001. Yaguarete Pora cut 60 km of roads into it after taking title to 78,000 hectares in 2002; conversion for pasture began in earnest by 2004-05, with the first large-scale clearing on a ranch in the south-east corner in 2005. Earthsight records Yaguarete Pora clearing more than 2,000 hectares under its 2007 licence, 5,500 hectares through 2014 and 2015, a further 2,000 hectares during 2015 and 900 hectares in 2017. Caucasian SA cleared 2,100 hectares in 2018 and 663 more in October and November 2019, and about 520 hectares were cleared in six weeks in the summer of 2019 at the ranch Chortitzer acquired that April. Global Forest Watch data showed at least two new cleared areas totalling around 100 hectares of densely forested land between 2020 and April 2021, and Earthsight counted more than 200 fires on Caucasian land in 2020 (Mongabay). Thirteen different ranches had obtained titles covering most of the reserve.
cx: Survival International on behalf of the Ayoreo people vs. Gruppo Pasubio
Gruppo Pasubio’s purchase of leather linked to illegal deforestation of Indigenous lands
cases.whole: What the clearing produced was pasture: some 530 square kilometres inside the reserve cleared and stocked with cattle by the end of 2019 (Earthsight). Paraguay's leather exports in January to April 2021 came to 9,424 metric tons, about a third more than the same months of 2020, and two of the three exporters linked to hides from the reserve increased their shipments to Italy after Earthsight's first report in September 2020 (Mongabay). Earthsight estimates that 39 per cent of Paraguay's leather exports are destined for Pasubio, which tanned hides for car interiors sold to BMW and Jaguar Land Rover. No figure was found for any payment to the Ayoreo Totobiegosode, and the land titles over most of the reserve remained in the ranches' hands.
